questions.prompt: What do Power BI tenant settings actually control, and what is the critical limitation Microsoft's own documentation states about them?
options: They turn whole features on or off, org-wide or for specific security groups — but per Microsoft's own documentation, they are not a security measure, since disabling a feature in the UI doesn't change what a user's underlying permissions already allow
They are a genuine security measure — disabling a feature such as Export data actually prevents anyone with read access to that data from obtaining it through any other means
They apply only inside Power BI Desktop and have no effect once a report is published to the service
They control which specific rows of a table a given role can see, the same mechanism row-level security uses
They are configured per workspace by that workspace's Admin, rather than tenant-wide by a tenant or Fabric admin
They take up to 15 minutes to apply, but can only ever be set to fully enabled or fully disabled for the whole organization — no per-group scoping exists
questions.explain: Tenant settings are the single biggest governance lever in Power BI — one admin screen that turns entire features on or off, org-wide or for specific security groups. But Microsoft's documentation is explicit that they are not a security measure: they control what the UI offers, not what a user's underlying permissions already allow. Real access control still requires workspace roles, item permissions, RLS, and OLS.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B states the exact misconception the lesson warns against directly. Disabling Export data on a semantic model does not stop a user who already has read access to that data from querying it and persisting the results through some other means — the tenant setting only removes that one button from the interface, it doesn't revoke the underlying permission.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of publishing a Power BI app, per Lesson 5, in the correct order.
items: Open the workspace and start Create app from the toolbar, beginning the Setup step with the app's name, description, logo, and theme
On the Content tab, explicitly add the specific reports, dashboards, and semantic models that should be included — nothing is added automatically
On the Audience tab, create one or more audience groups and set show/hide toggles for each item, per audience
Grant each audience access to either the entire organization or to specific people and groups
Select Publish app to push the packaged, read-only content out to its audiences
questions.explain: The app wizard always runs Setup (identity), then Content (what's included — never automatic), then Audience (who sees what, including the access grant for each audience), and only then Publish. Updating later follows the same shape: add to the workspace first, then explicitly update the app.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the four workspace roles, per Lesson 3.
options: Admin can update or delete the workspace and manage every user's role
A Member can add new users with lower permissions but cannot change the role of someone already in the workspace
Row-level security restricts what Admins, Members, and Contributors see, the same way it restricts Viewers
If a workspace has only one Admin, Power BI won't let that Admin remove themselves, since every workspace needs at least one
A Contributor can create, edit, and delete content, and can also manage who else has access to the workspace
questions.explain: Admin has full control, including managing every user's role. A Member can add lower-permission users but can't re-role an existing member — an Admin has to remove them first. Power BI always requires at least one Admin, so the sole Admin can't remove themselves. Row-level security only restricts the Viewer role; Admin, Member, and Contributor all have edit permission and see unfiltered data regardless of any RLS role. Contributor can create, edit, and delete content, but cannot manage access — that's an Admin or Member capability.

questions.prompt: Match each workspace structure term to what it actually is, per Lesson 4.
right: Hundreds of flat, unstructured workspaces created ad hoc with no organizing principle
A structural grouping of related workspaces by business area
A finer-grained grouping nested inside a domain, useful once that domain's own workspace count grows large
A consistent pattern like Team-Project-Environment that keeps workspace names self-documenting as the list grows
questions.explain: Workspace sprawl is the failure mode of hundreds of flat, unstructured workspaces. A domain groups related workspaces by business area; a subdomain narrows that grouping further once a domain itself grows large. A naming convention like Team-Project-Environment keeps individual workspace names self-documenting as the tenant scales.

questions.prompt: A BI team builds an RLS role meant to restrict 12 salespeople to only their own region's rows, then adds all 12 to the workspace as Members instead of Viewers. What actually happens when those salespeople open the report?
options: They see every row regardless of the RLS role, because RLS only restricts the Viewer role — Members have edit permission, and RLS doesn't apply to anyone with edit access
They see only their own region's rows, because RLS applies equally to every workspace role
They see no rows at all, because adding someone as a Member without assigning them to an RLS role blocks all access by default
They see every row, but only until an Admin manually re-applies the RLS role to Members
questions.explain: Row-level security only restricts the Viewer role. Admin, Member, and Contributor all have edit permission on the workspace's content, and RLS has zero effect on anyone with edit permission — they already have full access to the underlying data by virtue of their role. If RLS needs to actually restrict someone, that person has to be a Viewer.

questions.prompt: A semantic model connects to an on-premises SQL Server database through a gateway. Three weeks after setup, the service account's password is rotated in Active Directory, but nobody updates the credentials stored in Power BI. What happens to the scheduled refresh?
options: It begins failing on its next scheduled run, and continues failing silently until someone notices and updates the stored credentials in the semantic model's settings
It automatically picks up the new password the next time Active Directory syncs with the gateway
It keeps succeeding, because Power BI caches the data from the last successful refresh indefinitely
The gateway itself detects the rotation and emails every workspace Viewer a warning before the next refresh
questions.explain: Credentials are entered once and retained with the semantic model. If the underlying password changes, refresh starts failing silently until someone goes back into the settings pane and updates the credentials — password rotations and service account changes are the single most common cause of refresh failures, and nothing in Power BI auto-detects or auto-notifies on this.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an RLS role's DAX filter expression is written in Power BI ________, using the Modeling ribbon's Manage roles dialog — assigning actual members to that role happens afterward, in the Power BI service.
questions.explain: Roles are defined in Power BI Desktop, where a model author writes a DAX filter expression against a table. That role travels with the model when it's published. Assigning actual people or security groups to the role is a separate step that happens in the Power BI service, not Desktop.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about object-level security (OLS), per Lesson 8.
options: Setting a column's Object Level Security property to None hides it entirely from that role, as if it doesn't exist in the model at all
OLS roles are created and configured natively in Power BI Desktop's Modeling ribbon, the same place RLS roles are defined
A report visual that still references a column set to None for a role returns an error for that role's members, not a blank value
Read and Default behave identically for OLS purposes — both leave the object visible
Rolling out OLS on an existing, widely-used semantic model requires no review of existing reports, since hidden objects fail gracefully
questions.explain: None fully hides a table or column from a role, as if it doesn't exist. A visual, measure, or relationship still referencing that hidden object returns an error, not a blank, for members of that role — which is exactly why rolling out OLS means auditing every report for references to the newly hidden object first, not flipping the property and walking away. Read and Default are functionally the same (visible); Read just documents intent explicitly. Unlike RLS, Power BI Desktop has no native OLS editor — it historically requires an external tool like Tabular Editor.

questions.prompt: Match each sharing and permissions term to what it actually controls, per Lesson 9.
right: Grants access going forward via a selectable link type; doesn't show who already has access
Lets a recipient create new reports off the same underlying semantic model
The audit screen listing every link and direct share an item currently has, with revoke controls
Grants a workspace role (Admin, Member, Contributor, or Viewer) across everything in that workspace at once
questions.explain: Send link grants access going forward through a chosen link type, but doesn't show the full picture of who already has access. Manage permissions is the actual audit screen — every link and direct share, with revoke controls. Workspace access grants a role across the entire workspace, a broader and coarser grant than sharing one item. Build permission is the optional toggle letting a recipient create new content off the same semantic model.

questions.prompt: A tenant admin applies the "Highly Confidential" sensitivity label to a semantic model, and a teammate assumes this alone now prevents anyone without clearance from exporting the data. Based on Lesson 10, is that assumption correct?
options: Not necessarily — a sensitivity label always classifies the content, but it only enforces real protection like encryption or access limits if the tenant's label policy is configured to do so
Yes — every sensitivity label in Power BI always applies encryption and blocks export automatically, with no additional configuration required
No — sensitivity labels in Power BI are purely cosmetic and never trigger any real protection under any configuration
Yes, but only for dashboards — semantic models never carry any real enforcement regardless of tenant configuration
questions.explain: A sensitivity label is always a classification — a visible, auditable marker that travels with exports and downstream copies. Whether it also enforces real protection, such as encryption or access restriction, depends on how the tenant's label policy configures that specific label. Assuming a label alone locks content down is exactly the mistake Lesson 10 warns against; it classifies by default, and only enforces if the organization's policy says so.

questions.prompt: What does a Certified badge in Power BI actually represent, and who is allowed to apply it?
options: An organizational review signal — someone holding tenant-granted certifier rights has checked the content against the org's written certification criteria and is putting their name behind it
The same self-service signal as Promoted — any content owner can apply it without any special permission
A badge that's automatically applied once a dataset's usage metrics cross a certain number of views
A badge that only exists on apps, not on datasets or reports
A badge that, once applied, automatically enables row-level security on the underlying semantic model
A badge any workspace Viewer can apply to flag content they personally find trustworthy
questions.explain: Certified is an organizational signal: someone with recognized authority, holding certifier rights a tenant admin specifically granted, has checked the content against the org's written certification criteria — accuracy, a known owner, a documented refresh schedule — and is putting their name behind it. Power BI itself only enforces who's allowed to click the button; the review process is enforced by the organization outside the tool.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes Promoted, not Certified. Promoted really is the self-service badge any content owner can apply with no special permission. Certified is deliberately gated one level above it — it stays grayed out for most users until a tenant admin grants certifier rights, which is the entire reason the course treats the two as separate tiers rather than one badge.

questions.prompt: A governance reviewer wants to know exactly how many downstream reports and workspaces depend on a certified dataset before changing its refresh schedule, and wants a one-click way to warn every affected owner. Which tool actually does this, and why not the other one?
options: Impact analysis — lineage view only shows the connections as a diagram, with no running total of impacted items and no way to notify anyone
Lineage view — impact analysis only works on dataflows, never on semantic models
Either tool works identically, since impact analysis is just a renamed version of lineage view
Usage metrics — it's the only one of the three that lists which workspaces depend on a dataset
questions.explain: Lineage view shows connections as a diagram, which is useful for understanding structure, but it doesn't total up the blast radius in numbers or let you message anyone. Impact analysis is the dedicated view built for exactly that: it counts every impacted child item, groups them by type or workspace, and has a one-click Notify contacts action that emails every contact across every impacted workspace before a change ships.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about usage metrics and the audit log, per Lessons 14 and 15.
options: The Views by user table in a usage metrics report ties usage to specific named individuals, not just a total view count
Usage metrics and the audit log answer the exact same question, just at different time ranges
A certified dataset with zero recent views in its usage metrics is a signal worth investigating, not something to ignore
Power BI's activity auditing runs through Microsoft Purview's unified audit log, the same system used tenant-wide across Microsoft 365
Audit search results can only be viewed once, immediately after running the search, and can't be saved for later review
questions.explain: Views by user names exactly who viewed a report, not just a total. A certified-but-unviewed dataset is a red flag — either it's genuinely obsolete or people have quietly moved to an uncertified substitute, either way worth investigating. Power BI's auditing runs through Microsoft Purview's unified audit log. Usage metrics and the audit log answer different questions at different scopes — usage metrics is one report's view counts; the audit log is who did what, to which item, tenant-wide. Audit searches are saved as jobs with their own status and can be reviewed again later, not viewed only once.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: before a single dataset can be certified, a tenant admin must enable the ________ setting, which also decides whether certifier rights are open to everyone, restricted to specific security groups, or delegated to domain admins.
questions.explain: Certification is off, and gated, until a tenant admin deliberately turns on the Certification setting. That one setting answers the most important governance question about certification before a single dataset is touched: who is allowed to certify?

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order for safely changing a certified dataset, per Lesson 13.
items: Open lineage view to see the certified dataset's upstream and downstream connections as a diagram
Select the dataset's impact-analysis icon to open the dedicated impact analysis pane
Review the number of impacted child items, grouped by item type or by workspace
Use Notify contacts to warn every contact across every impacted workspace before making the change
Make the change to the certified dataset
questions.explain: Lineage view first confirms the dependency chain exists at all. Impact analysis then turns that diagram into an actual count of impacted items and workspaces. Notify contacts warns every affected owner before anything changes. Only after that does the actual change to the certified dataset happen — reversing this order defeats the entire point of running impact analysis beforehand.

questions.prompt: A team creates a deployment pipeline and names its three stages Development, Test, and Production. Under the hood, what does each of those three stages actually consist of?
options: Each stage is a separate, real Power BI workspace assigned to that stage — the same workspace roles, tenant settings, and sensitivity labels from earlier chapters still apply to each one individually
All three stages are folders inside one shared workspace, distinguished only by a tag
Each stage is a snapshot of the same workspace's content at a different point in time, not a separate workspace
Only the Production stage is a real workspace — Development and Test are temporary, in-memory previews
questions.explain: A deployment pipeline doesn't create some new kind of container — it's a wrapper around three ordinary Power BI workspaces. Whatever you name the stages, each one is backed by its own separate, real workspace, and every governance mechanism from earlier chapters — workspace roles, tenant settings, sensitivity labels — still applies to each stage's workspace individually.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about comparing and deploying between pipeline stages, per Lesson 17.
options: An item marked "Only in source" exists in the source stage but hasn't been deployed to the destination stage yet
The deploy confirmation dialog can be configured to continue deploying the rest of a batch even if one item fails
Comparing items before deploying is optional and happens automatically only after the deploy action completes
A dataflow marked "Only in source" when comparing Test against Development means it already exists identically in both stages
Most teams leave the "continue even if items fail" checkbox unchecked when a batch includes a certified dataset, so one failure doesn't let a broken item through alongside good ones
questions.explain: "Only in source" means the item exists in the source stage (e.g., Development) but hasn't reached the destination stage (e.g., Test) yet — not that it matches in both. The deploy dialog does offer a checkbox to continue even if one or more items fail, but most teams leave it unchecked for a batch including a certified dataset, so one failure doesn't silently let a broken item through. Comparison happens before deploying, specifically so a reviewer can catch exactly this kind of issue before approving — it isn't something that only runs after the fact.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a deployment pipeline doesn't create some new kind of container — it's a wrapper around three ordinary Power BI ________ you likely already know how to govern.
questions.explain: Development, Test, and Production are each a real, separate Power BI workspace assigned to that stage. The pipeline itself is just the wrapper connecting them — all the governance you already know for an individual workspace still applies to each one.

questions.prompt: Match each item on the tenant-wide governance status dashboard to the earlier-chapter idea it rolls up, per Lesson 18.
left: Items with description / items by last access date
right: Chapter 1's workspace and structure concepts, now rolled up tenant-wide
The documentation and usage-metrics ideas from earlier chapters, applied estate-wide instead of to one report
The sensitivity labeling work from Chapter 2, now tracked as a tenant-wide completion number
Lessons 11-12's endorsement and certification, pointed at the whole tenant instead of one dataset
questions.explain: "Items with description" and "items by last access date" are the documentation and usage-metrics ideas from earlier chapters, scaled estate-wide. Label coverage is Chapter 2's sensitivity labeling, now a tenant-wide completion number. "Establish sources of truth" is Lessons 11-12's endorsement and certification, pointed at the whole tenant. Domain, workspace, and item counts are Chapter 1's structure concepts, rolled up to tenant scale.

questions.prompt: In the Meridian Outdoor Supply case study, the governance team's first move was consolidating three duplicate "Weekly Sales Flash" copies into one workspace and dataset — before certifying anything or touching a deployment pipeline. Why did consolidation have to come first?
options: Certifying one dataset, or building a pipeline around it, is pointless while two uncertified duplicate copies still exist elsewhere — the duplicates would keep producing conflicting numbers regardless of what happens to the one dataset that got certified
Consolidation is required by Power BI before row-level security can be configured on any semantic model
A deployment pipeline technically cannot be created until a dataset already holds a Certified badge
Certification and consolidation are unrelated steps that could have happened in either order with the same result
questions.explain: The actual problem was three competing copies of the same number, not that any one copy lacked a badge or a pipeline. Certifying one of the three without retiring the other two would leave the other two still circulating and still producing different numbers in different decks — the trust and lifecycle work from Chapters 3 and 4 only pays off once there's a single source left to apply it to.
